estimate.text: An estimator is a function T of the random sample; its estimate applies the same function to the observed sample.
estimate.title: Estimator and realized estimate

bias.text: Bias is the expected estimator minus the true parameter. An unbiased estimator has zero bias.
bias.title: Bias and unbiasedness

mse.text: Mean squared error equals estimator variance plus squared bias.
mse.title: Bias–variance decomposition

consistency.text: Consistency means that for every fixed positive tolerance, the probability of missing the parameter by more than that tolerance tends to zero as sample size increases.
consistency.title: Consistency in probability

consistency-sufficient.text: By Markov applied to squared error, the error probability is at most variance plus squared bias divided by tolerance squared. If both variance and bias tend to zero, consistency follows.
consistency-sufficient.title: A sufficient condition for consistency

sample-mean.text: For IID observations with mean mu and finite variance sigma squared, the sample mean is unbiased and its variance is sigma squared over n.
sample-mean.title: Properties of the sample mean

weighted-mean.text: The variance of a fixed weighted mean is sigma squared times the sum of squared weights, at least sigma squared over n.
weighted-mean.title: Equal weights minimize variance in this class

cauchy.text: Cauchy–Schwarz implies the sum of squared weights is at least one over n, with equality for equal weights.
cauchy.title: Cauchy–Schwarz proof

sample-variance.text: Sample variance uses the sum of squared deviations from the sample mean divided by n minus one. It is unbiased under IID finite-variance sampling.
sample-variance.title: Unbiased sample variance

variance-identity.text: The residual sum of squares equals the squared deviations from the true mean minus n times the squared estimation error of the sample mean.
variance-identity.title: Residual sum-of-squares identity

variance-proof.text: Taking expectations of the identity gives n sigma squared minus sigma squared, or n minus one times sigma squared. Dividing by n minus one proves unbiasedness.
variance-proof.title: Proof of the n minus one correction

second-moment.text: Equivalently, subtract the second moment of the sample mean from the second moment of an observation and multiply by n over n minus one.
second-moment.title: Equivalent second-moment derivation

estimated-se.text: The true standard error uses population sigma; its usual estimate substitutes sample standard deviation S.
estimated-se.title: Estimating the standard error

binary-mean.text: Sample proportion p is K over n, is unbiased for pi, and has variance pi times one minus pi over n.
binary-mean.title: Bernoulli estimation

binary-variance.text: The plug-in variance p times one minus p is biased downward; multiply it by n over n minus one to obtain the unbiased sample variance.
binary-variance.title: Plug-in versus unbiased binary variance

binary-se.text: The usual plug-in SE is the square root of p times one minus p over n. An unbiased estimator of the variance of p uses n minus one instead.
binary-se.title: Two different variance estimators

z-pivot.text: Under IID normal sampling with known sigma, the standardized sample mean is standard normal. z sub alpha over two is the positive upper-tail critical value.
z-pivot.title: Normal pivot and tail convention

z-ci.tex: \overline X\pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},\qquad ME=z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},\qquad w=2ME
z-ci.text: The known-sigma interval is sample mean plus or minus the normal critical value times sigma over square root n. Its width is twice the margin of error.
z-ci.title: Known-variance confidence interval

z-proof.tex: \begin{aligned}P\!\left(-z_{\alpha/2}\leq\frac{\overline X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\leq z_{\alpha/2}\right)&=1-\alpha\\P\!\left(\overline X-z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\leq\mu\leq\overline X+z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right)&=1-\alpha.\end{aligned}
z-proof.text: Start with the central probability of the standard normal pivot. Multiply by sigma over square root n and rearrange to isolate mu between random endpoints.
z-proof.title: Deriving the confidence interval

t-pivot.tex: T=\frac{\overline X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1},\qquad \overline X\pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac{S}{\sqrt n}
t-pivot.text: For IID normal data, the studentized mean has a Student t distribution with n minus one degrees of freedom. Use its upper-tail alpha-over-two critical value times estimated SE.
t-pivot.title: Unknown-variance t interval

wald.text: The Wald interval for a population proportion uses the observed proportion plus or minus a normal critical value times the plug-in standard error.
wald.title: Large-sample Wald interval

wilson.text: Wilson interval has adjusted center p plus z squared over two n divided by one plus z squared over n, and the displayed adjusted half-width.
wilson.title: Wilson score interval

plan-mean.text: To make the known-sigma margin at most e, use the ceiling of z squared times sigma squared divided by e squared.
plan-mean.title: Planning a mean sample size

plan-proportion.text: Use a planning proportion p zero in the normal-approximation sample-size formula. Its variance is maximized at one half.
plan-proportion.title: Planning a proportion sample size

precision-tradeoff.text: Sample size is inversely proportional to squared margin. At 95 percent with planning proportion one half, the rounded-z formula is about 0.9604 over margin squared.
precision-tradeoff.title: Precision has a square-law cost
